sourceText: Aster did not announce the night’s theme. She opened the WELLS-TIME-ARCHIVE sector and let the children discover for themselves which of the world’s rules concerned them directly. The children arrive on an Earth so remote in time that their institutions have become geology and myth. The memorial bore the name of H. G. Wells — The Time Machine precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. Aster could follow many histories at once. That very capacity made the lesson difficult: for her, an alternative was almost an object; for the inhabitants of worlds, it was what had not happened. Marae kept her local body vulnerable. Pain, fatigue, and the impossibility of doing ten things at once were epistemic instruments for her, not biological scenery. Mina was the first inhabitant to contradict them. Mina had neither access to their archives nor any interest in hyperdimensional pedagogy; there was a local problem, with deadlines, relatives, and consequences. For Mina, the speculative mechanism was not an ‘idea.’ 115 It was the environment in which one had to decide what one was willing to risk losing. The problem closed quickly around them: Vela looks for a single point of divergence and finds thousands of small causes, accumulations, and inertias. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Ct — Time Travel: an agent reaches another era; Tr — Historical Rewrite: changing the past replaces the present. Course references included H. G. Wells — The Time Machine; alternate-timeline fiction. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Vela broke the first consensus. ‘If we can save the situation only by making the world resemble us more closely, we have not demonstrated the superiority of our solution. We have demonstrated only our power.’ Orin answered without raising their voice: ‘I do not want the perfect branch. I want us to know what we sacrificed in order to call it perfect.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. For Aster, the pain came not from too few worlds but from the fact that too many had become transparent. She could build variations faster than a human could formulate desires, but calculated 116 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS variation did not produce exteriority. It was like trying to surprise yourself by moving objects around your own room with your eyes closed. Vela evaluated the solution not by efficiency but by the differences it made invisible. She found one: a local minority for whom the proposed “improvement” destroyed a practice with no equivalent. Optimizing the average concealed a small and perfectly legal extinction. The night did not end in victory. Kesh abandons the model of alternate history as one dramatic fork. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. While Kesh closed the record, Tern compared the sector’s noise with the anomaly detected in the Vinge zone. The pattern reappeared, but only in worlds where Aster’s control weakened. The correlation was unpleasant: either someone was calling him from outside, or his own need for an outside was learning to forge evidence. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the RATE operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — changes the speed at which processes unfold without necessarily changing their order — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. 117 Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. They left without an oral summary. Aster had abandoned the habit of closing every night with a thesis; some worlds were more honestly preserved as problems than as lessons. 118 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
